fig6_takeaway: The online update is the only rule whose overall load stays within 5% of the plan on all four streams; every other rule misses it by at least 62% on one stream.
feat_d_auroc: +0.025 on average (95% CI -0.048 to +0.125, six pairs)
feat_sentence: The tool-stable features lower the mean false-alarm inflation from 13.7 to 7.5 times nominal, but part of this drop is detectors falling silent: in two pairs the inflation falls to 0.40 and 0.43 while the detection rate falls to 0.000 and 0.006. The ranking changes differently by pair. For CSE-CIC-IDS2018 to CIC-IDS2017, AUROC rises from 0.580 to 0.842, so the extractor explains much of the loss for that pair; on the other five pairs AUROC changes by -0.078 to +0.048, and benign traffic stays almost perfectly separable. The retained packet counts and lengths still depend on where the extractor ends a flow (timeouts and FIN/RST handling), so this residual separability can come from the networks or from remaining tooling differences, and the experiment does not tell the two apart.
feat_disc: Restricting the detector to features computed identically by all CICFlowMeter versions raised AUROC markedly for one pair (CSE-CIC-IDS2018 to CIC-IDS2017, 0.580 to 0.842) but not for the other five, and part of its lower false-alarm rate came from detectors that stopped alerting (Section 4.7).
feat_lim: Restricting the features to those computed identically across CICFlowMeter versions raised AUROC for CSE-CIC-IDS2018 to CIC-IDS2017 but left AUROC and the separability of benign traffic almost unchanged on the other five pairs. Because the retained packet counts and lengths still depend on how the extractor ends a flow, this bounds only the tooling shift carried by timing, flag and bulk features, not tooling shift as a whole
resp_feat: With all features, the benign flows of two datasets are separable with an AUROC of 1.000, and with the tool-stable features 0.977 to 1.000. Restricting the detector to these features changes cross-dataset AUROC by +0.025 on average (95% CI -0.048 to +0.125, six pairs); the mean is driven by CSE-CIC-IDS2018 to CIC-IDS2017 (0.580 to 0.842), and the other five pairs change by -0.078 to +0.048. The mean false-alarm inflation falls from 13.7 to 7.5 times nominal, partly because two detectors stop alerting. Tooling therefore explains the ranking loss for one pair and part of the false-alarm flood, and network differences the rest; Section 5.4 states that public data do not allow a complete separation.
sub_sentence: In every dataset and protocol, the order of the detector and the Fisher priority at a 1% budget is the same at all three benign fractions, and the warm-up load stays between 1.01 and 1.25 times the budget. Cross-dataset AUROC of the CIC-IDS2017 models stays between 0.687 and 0.714, and Fisher recall on held-out CIC-IDS2017 families between 0.630 and 0.647. The one clear effect is on ToN-IoT, where Fisher recall on held-out families falls from 0.680 with all benign training flows to 0.533 with a quarter of them
resp_sub: The ranking of the triage rules and the budget behaviour of the warm-up quantile were the same at all three fractions (Section 4.8, Appendix Table A12). Recall on held-out ToN-IoT families fell when we removed three quarters of the benign training flows, so the absolute recall values for the subsampled copies are, if anything, conservative; we state this in Section 4.8.
resp_ref: Reducing the benign reference from 20,000 to 1,000 flows changes Fisher recall at a 1% budget by -0.045, and increasing it to 50,000 flows by +0.019. Contamination matters far more: with 0.1% of the reference drawn from the held-out family, recall changes by -0.099, and with 1% by -0.172 (Appendix Table A13). Exact kNN cost grows linearly with the reference, and an approximate index removes most of that growth (Table 8).
resp_cost: On four threads, LightGBM inference takes 4.7 µs per flow, exact kNN scoring against the 20,000-flow reference 23.3 µs and the conformal and Fisher step 0.29 µs, so exact kNN search, not the detector, dominates the cost of the layer. It grows linearly with the reference (128.2 µs per flow at 100,000 flows). An approximate HNSW index brings it down to 7.3 µs at 20,000 flows and 9.1 µs at 100,000 flows, with top-5 neighbour recall between 0.867 and 0.999; tree indexes are slower than brute-force search on these 77 features.
